How Do Unusual Items Influence Profit?

To properly understand Ecovyst's profit results, we need to consider the US$17m expense attributed to unusual items. While deductions due to unusual items are disappointing in the first instance, there is a silver lining. We looked at thousands of listed companies and found that unusual items are very often one-off in nature. And that's hardly a surprise given these line items are considered unusual. If Ecovyst doesn't see those unusual expenses repeat, then all else being equal we'd expect its profit to increase over the coming year.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Because of this, we think Ecovyst's earnings potential is at least as good as it seems, and maybe even better! And on top of that, its earnings per share have grown at an extremely impressive rate over the last year. The goal of this article has been to assess how well we can rely on the statutory earnings to reflect the company's potential, but there is plenty more to consider. data.description:

The shares cost US$229 at the start of the period, so any view on Applied Materials had to square that price with very different stories about AI hardware demand and China risk.

On the optimistic side, the April 2025 Narrative pointed to a Fair Value of US$250, a price implied by expectations of 7.8% annual revenue growth and rising profit margins as advanced AI and IoT chip architectures required more complex equipment and services.

The more cautious November 2025 view suggested a Fair Value of US$195, based on 4.3% revenue growth assumptions and concern that export restrictions on Chinese customers could weigh on future orders even as AI related projects expanded.

Applied Materials reported Q4 2026 revenue of US$10,409 million and net income of US$2,718 million, both above Q4 2025 levels. The net margin slipping from 27.9% to 26.1% cut against the most upbeat margin expansion story, so the evidence mainly backed the optimistic case but with a profitability caveat.

The lesson for other stocks is simple. When you see a bullish pitch built on operating leverage, check whether revenue and absolute profit improve without the margin percentage quietly moving the wrong way in the reported numbers.

data.title: Is Coinbase Global (COIN) Undervalued After Wirex Put Tokenized Stocks On Base?
data.description:
Wirex’s launch of tokenized U.S. equities on Coinbase’s Base network places Coinbase Global (COIN) more deeply into the plumbing of onchain finance, linking its infrastructure to 24/7 stock exposure for millions of users.

For investors watching the ticker, Coinbase Global’s share price has come under pressure, with a 1 day share price return that declined 4.02%, a 30 day share price return that fell 33.58%, and a year to date share price return that dropped 51.37%. The 3 year total shareholder return remains positive at 9.03%, while the 1 year total shareholder return declined 56.06%. This points to fading short term momentum despite onchain moves like Wirex’s tokenized stocks launch and Coinbase’s recent work on tokenized rights, futures products, and post quantum custody.

Spot opportunities across onchain finance by scanning our hand picked 21 cryptocurrency and blockchain stocks, which, like Coinbase Global, sits at the intersection of tokenization, trading access, and blockchain infrastructure.

Coinbase Global is pushing deeper into tokenized finance while its own stock has been under clear pressure. The platform story looks strong. The price you pay for that exposure is the real question.

Most Popular Narrative: 54% Undervalued

Against a last close of $115.02, the most followed narrative on Coinbase Global pegs fair value at $247.39, framing the recent share price slide as a potential disconnect rather than a verdict on the business model.

The simplest way I can think about it is that Coinbase behaves a bit like a leveraged crypto proxy. If crypto prices rise materially over the next 5 to 10 years, Coinbase’s earnings power could expand much faster than the underlying asset because a lot of the operating base should be relatively stable.

See why 28 investors see Coinbase Global as 54% undervalued.

The view from QuanD, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, hinges on whether crypto becomes a much larger asset class over time, with Coinbase Global collecting more fees as volumes, custody balances, and subscription products scale on a relatively fixed cost base.

This storyline sits alongside the data. Coinbase Global reported revenue of $5.44b with an annual revenue growth rate of 15.70%, while still posting a net loss of $701.62m and a negative return on equity. Forecasts point to earnings growth of 63.16% per year and a path to profitability within three years, although the business is currently unprofitable and its future return on equity is expected to reach 13.5%, which screens as relatively low against higher quality benchmarks.

Analysts as a group have a price target around $195.00, which is 41.02% above the last close, but the data shows that this group is not within a statistically tight band of agreement. That lack of consensus underlines how much of the valuation work still comes back to an investor’s own conviction on long term crypto adoption and how Coinbase Global monetises that through trading, custody, and subscription lines.

Result: Fair Value of $247.39 (UNDERVALUED)

Still, the Coinbase Global narrative can break if crypto adoption stalls or if regulators restrict key revenue lines and compress fee based earnings power.

Another View: Coinbase Global Through Sales Multiples

There is a very different message coming from simple sales ratios. Coinbase Global trades on a P/S of 5.6x, which looks expensive against the US Capital Markets industry at 3.3x and also above its own fair ratio of 4.1x that the market could move toward over time.

Peers are even richer at 10.6x P/S, so the stock screens cheaper than that group, yet still carries valuation risk if revenue or sentiment weakens and the multiple drifts closer to the fair ratio.

data.title: Sweetgreen's (NYSE:SG) Earnings Are Built On Soft Foundations
data.description:
Shareholders were pleased with the recent earnings report from Sweetgreen, Inc. (NYSE:SG). Despite this, we feel that there are some reasons to be cautious with these earnings.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Zooming In On Sweetgreen's Earnings

One key financial ratio used to measure how well a company converts its profit to free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

For the year to September 2026, Sweetgreen had an accrual ratio of 0.44. Statistically speaking, that's a real negative for future earnings. And indeed, during the period the company didn't produce any free cash flow whatsoever. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of US$108m, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of US$19.1m. We also note that Sweetgreen's free cash flow was actually negative last year as well, so we could understand if shareholders were bothered by its outflow of US$108m. Having said that, there is more to the story. We can see that unusual items have impacted its statutory profit, and therefore the accrual ratio. The good news for shareholders is that Sweetgreen's accrual ratio was much better last year, so this year's poor reading might simply be a case of a short term mismatch between profit and FCF. As a result, some shareholders may be looking for stronger cash conversion in the current year.

See our latest analysis for Sweetgreen

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

The Impact Of Unusual Items On Profit

Given the accrual ratio, it's not overly surprising that Sweetgreen's profit was boosted by unusual items worth US$150m in the last twelve months. While it's always nice to have higher profit, a large contribution from unusual items sometimes dampens our enthusiasm. When we crunched the numbers on thousands of publicly listed companies, we found that a boost from unusual items in a given year is often not repeated the next year. And that's as you'd expect, given these boosts are described as 'unusual'. Sweetgreen had a rather significant contribution from unusual items relative to its profit to September 2026. As a result, we can surmise that the unusual items are making its statutory profit significantly stronger than it would otherwise be.

Our Take On Sweetgreen's Profit Performance

Sweetgreen had a weak accrual ratio, but its profit did receive a boost from unusual items. On reflection, the above-mentioned factors give us the strong impression that Sweetgreen'sunderlying earnings power is not as good as it might seem, based on the statutory profit numbers. data.title: Apple (AAPL) Heads To French Trial In June 2027 Over iPhone Repairs
data.description:
• Apple (NasdaqGS:AAPL) is scheduled to face a French trial in June 2027 over alleged planned obsolescence of iPhones.
  • French prosecutors accuse Apple of limiting third-party iPhone repairs through design choices and software practices.
  • Consumer groups in France are seeking fines and compensation related to the alleged restriction of independent repair options.
  • The French planned obsolescence trial over third party iPhone repairs aligns with broader themes identified in our research. Our analysis turns up 2 other big wins for Apple as well.

Consider widening your watchlist to include other large tech stocks with similar regulatory themes by reviewing 41 AI small caps.

Apple, a US tech giant with a market cap of about $5.1 trillion, builds an integrated ecosystem of iPhones, Macs, iPads, wearables, and accessories, which makes any legal scrutiny of its repair practices especially relevant for how its hardware and services operate together.

Does the team leading Apple have what it takes? See our full breakdown of the management team's track record and compensation.

What exactly is Apple being taken to court for in France?

French prosecutors allege that Apple made it harder or impossible for independent repair shops to fix certain iPhone models between November 2021 and July 2024. The case focuses on design and software decisions that are said to restrict third party repairs, which consumer groups argue shortened practical device lifespans and limited choice for users.

Does this French trial change the current Apple Narrative for investors?

The Narrative already flags legal overhangs as a key constraint alongside high memory costs and execution changes under the new CEO. A planned obsolescence case tied directly to iPhone repair policies fits that risk bucket, because any tighter repair rules or penalties could make it harder for Apple to support higher priced, AI centric hardware without extra cost or complexity.

See how these catalysts shape Apple's path to a $339 fair value.

What should you watch next to gauge the real impact on Apple?

The clearest check will be Apple’s formal response and any interim rulings or settlements before the June 2027 Paris trial date, especially if they force changes to repair terms across Europe. Concrete signals to track are whether Apple expands parts access, loosens software pairing for third party repairs, or books specific provisions for potential fines and compensation.
